paragraphs: Hatztzali en tzarik melicha, lepi shehaesh shoeb haddam shebbo meatzmo belo melicha; lepikak bemaqom sheen melach matzuy, yitzleh habbasar veaach"k yukal lebashshelo - veken osim ellu hashshotin mashqeh sammanin sheqqorin "isba" (eseb lehargaat merotz haddam), sheen okelim shum dabar sheyyesh bo melach kol zeman sheshshotim mashqeh zeh - sheyyaasu kak, litzlot habbasar, veaach"k yebashsheluhu kirtzonam. veim tzolehu "g haggechalim mammash, "p sheen meqom avir chalal ben hatztzali legechalim kede sheyyazub haddam, let lan bah, demikkol maqom nura mashab shaab haddam, veeno mannicho lachazor lehibbala babbasar; velo od, ella apillu tzolehu al haqqarqa shel hattannur shehu garup veqatum, deen kan esh beayin ella charso shel tannur hu cham meod veroteach, shari; mippene shettoqep hachom lebaddo hu sorep, vela chayeshinan shemma achar shenniplat haddam chozer ubolea, vekannizkar bapposeqim za"l; veayyen lehaggaon chiqre leb, yoreh dea, cheleq , siman l"v, dap n"h, v"yd-eprayim", siman t"v. vahagam dehaggaon htzl"ch bipsachim, resh pereq tzolin mechalleq ben al yede haesh atzmo leben hachom bilbad - yesh lismok al rubba demattirin; mihu, en lehattir litzlot habbasar betok hammachabat beli shum mashqeh "p shehi al haesh vechamma kemo gechalim mammash; vehattaam, mippene shehi keli, vela chashib zeh tzeliyya vekannizkar bechiqre lb za"l sham, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: Meat roasted over fire does not require salting beforehand, since the fire itself draws out and expels the blood from the meat without needing salt. Therefore, where there is no salt, one may roast the meat first and only afterward cook it. This is likewise how people who drank a certain medicinal beverage ("ashva") and were forbidden to eat anything with salt while taking it would behave — they would roast the meat first, and only afterward cook it as they wished. Even if the meat is roasted directly on the coals themselves, with no air gap through which blood could drip out, this causes no harm, since in any case the fire draws out the blood and does not let it be reabsorbed into the meat. And even if roasted on the very hot floor of an oven (with no actual fire, only intense heat from the clay), this is permitted, since the heat itself is what burns out and expels the blood, with no concern the blood will be reabsorbed. There is a dissenting opinion (the Gaon Tzelach) distinguishing between actual fire and mere heat, but the halacha leans toward the majority of lenient authorities. Nevertheless, it is forbidden to roast meat in a pan (with no liquid), even though it is as hot as actual coals — since a pan is a vessel, and roasting in a vessel is not considered "roasting" for this purpose.
takeaways: Roasted meat requires no salting — the fire itself draws out the blood.
Roasting directly on coals or on a very hot oven floor is permitted and effective like ordinary roasting; but roasting in a pan without liquid is forbidden, since a vessel is not considered roasting.

paragraphs: Ha deamerinan nura mashab shaab, haynu davqa dam hamkunnas babbasar shehu odennu beqirbo velo yatza adayin; abal im dam acher natap al habbasar, hinneh bazeh adderabba, teba haesh lehablia zeh haddam betok habbasar veeno shoeb oto; mihu, ledaat mera"n za"l disbira lehu, chom shehayyad soledet bo, im hu belo roteb kegon tzali o apuy o mebushshal, eno oser ella kede netila, vekannizkar besiman q"h, gam haka eno oser betzali ella kede netila. uledaat mvr"m za"l sham, debae shishshim, gam haka oser ad shishshim; lepikak im natap al hatztzali dam - ben shehu natap alayv beshaa shehu etzel haesh, uben shennatap alayv keshehaya tzonen - hare zeh oser ledidan, deazelinan batar mera"n za"l, kede netila; ulehaashkenazzim, deazeli batar mvr"m za"l, ad shishshim. veken hu haddin im natap alayv achar shehesiro min haesh beodo cham harbeh kechom shehaya bo al haesh, name dina haki; veayyen "kareti", siman "v, seip qatan '.

clarification.explanation: The rule that "the fire draws out the blood" is true only for blood that was trapped inside the meat itself and had not yet emerged. But if external blood (from another source) dripped onto the meat, the opposite is true in such a case: the fire will actually "seal in" and draw this blood into the meat, rather than drawing it out. There is a dispute here regarding severity: according to Maran (the Shulchan Aruch), if the heat was such that a hand would be burned by it but there is no sauce (as in roasting, baking, or cooking), the meat is not entirely forbidden but only requires cutting away and removing a bit ("to the thickness of a peeling"). According to the Rema, nullification in sixty against the dripped blood is required. Therefore, following the Sephardic custom (Maran), a small cut suffices; following the Ashkenazic custom (the Rema), sixty against the blood is required. The law is the same whether the blood dripped onto the meat while it was on the fire or while it was cold, and likewise if it dripped after the meat was removed from the fire while still very hot.
takeaways: The fire draws out only blood that was trapped inside the meat itself; external blood dripped onto it is instead sealed inward by the fire.
For Sephardim (Maran) it suffices to cut away the spot where blood dripped; for Ashkenazim (the Rema), nullification in sixty is required.

paragraphs: Im gebina qara velecha napela al hatztzali beodo cham, tzerika haggebina qelipa, mippene shebbalea min habbasar; d"g dela paleta - bolaat taam basar, vekannizkar b"shiyyure-beraka" beshem "chavvot-yair" za"l.

clarification.explanation: If a cold, moist piece of cheese fell onto roasting meat while it was still hot, the cheese must be peeled (its outer layer that touched the meat removed), since although the cheese did not release its taste into the meat (being cold), it did absorb and take in meat flavor from the hot roast — and therefore the part that touched must be removed.
takeaways: Cold cheese that touched hot meat — the meat need not be affected, but the cheese must be peeled, since it absorbed meat flavor from it.

paragraphs: "g deamarnu: hatztzali en tzarik melicha, mikkol maqom hamminhag lepazzer alayv melach meat keshehu tachub beshappud, vetzoleh oto tekep umiyyad kede shello yitmalle hammelach sheppizzeru alayv middam. veayyen mishbetzot zahab, seip qatan d'. vetzarik lehazhir bazeh, ki yesh nashim atzlaniyyot, veachar sheyyepazzeru alayv melach, shohin hatztzeliyya im yizdammen lahem eseq acher. vetzarik lehazhiram od: ben betzali zeh, ben betzali shetztzalu oto belo melach kelal - shello yegalgelo hashshepud tamid, abal beaqray, let lan bah. veayyen "minchat-yaaqob", kelal t', seip qatan v', vesipte daat, seip qatan y"b ushear acharonim. veotam sheshshotin mashqeh sheqqorin "isba", shemmaqpidim shello yannichu melach al habbasar kelal, yekolim litzloto belo pizzur melach techilla apillu dabar muat.

clarification.explanation: Although it was stated that roasted meat does not require salting, the custom is nevertheless to scatter a bit of salt on the meat while it is already skewered, and to roast it immediately — so the salt scattered on it does not have time to be absorbed with blood before the fire manages to draw it out. One must be especially careful of women who are careless: after scattering the salt, they sometimes delay due to some other task before beginning to roast — and this is problematic. One should also be warned not to keep turning the skewer constantly (whether with meat that has salt scattered on it or meat roasted with no salt at all), but only occasionally at intervals. One who drinks the aforementioned medicinal beverage and places no salt at all on the meat may roast it without scattering salt at the outset.
takeaways: It is customary to scatter a little salt on the roast just before roasting it immediately — so the fire draws out the blood before the salt absorbs it.
One must be careful not to delay after scattering the salt, and not to turn the skewer without pause.

paragraphs: Basar zeh shetztzolin belo melicha, o im molecho meat - keshettochabo bishpud vetzolehu miyyad, hinneh im ratza lebashshelo achar tzeliyyato, tzarik lehizzaher litzloto tzeliyya gemura, dehaynu kol tzarekko, vela saggi bachatzi tzeliyyato, deken hu daat mera"n za"l; v"g dmvr"m za"l sober desaggi bachatzi tzeliyyato - anan batar maran za"l geriran. v"p depoh irenu nohagim bakkabed shetztzolin oto chatzi tzeliyyato veaach"k mebashshelim oto - en lilmod din habbasar middin hakkabed, deyesh lomar: davqa bakkabed nahagu bekak, mishshum d"g dekabed yesh lo ribbuy dam yoter, im kol zeh rakkik hu tepe min habbasar, ubachatzi tzeliyya dideh poel haesh yoter mechatzi tzeliyya shel habbasar. veod, degam bakkabed en minhag barur vechazaq, yaan ki dabar zeh enam osim ella bebatte haaniyyim, sheyyebashshelu hakkabed achar hatztzeliyya; verob bene-adam okelin hakkabed tzali, umiuta demiuta hem hambashshelim oto, veyesh lomar mechesron yedia nahagu kak veen zeh minhag vatiqin. ulekak rauy lehorot lahem sheggam hakkabed yitzluhu tzeliyya gemura kesherotzim lebashshelo; vekol shekken habbasar shennitzla belo melicha shetztzarik litzloto tzeliyya gemura, ukedaat mera"n za"l; mihu, otam sheshshotim mashqeh sheqqorin "isba", shekkol tabshil shellahem bizman sheshshotim mashqeh hannizkar, shehu meshek sheloshim o arbaim yom, kullo mibbasar tzaluy - yesh lehaqel lahem litzloto chatzi tzeliyya ulebashshelo, mippene sheim tzolin oto tzeliyya gemura, lo yihyeh taam basar battabshil, sheyyazub shumman habbasar bitzliyya; vekevan deshotin zeh bishbil choli, yesh lehaqel lahem.

clarification.explanation: If one wishes to take meat that was roasted without salting (or with a little salt scattered right before immediate roasting), and afterward cook it — it must be fully and completely roasted, and a half-roasting does not suffice, since this is Maran's (the Shulchan Aruch's) view. The Rema disagrees and holds that a half-roasting suffices, but Sephardim follow Maran. In some places it was customary regarding liver to roast it only halfway and then cook it, but one should not derive from this a rule for ordinary meat, since liver is softer than meat and the fire acts more effectively on it even in a half-roasting, and furthermore this custom regarding liver is not a well-established, clear one — most people in any case eat liver roasted rather than cooked, and only a few (mainly the poor) cook it after a half-roasting, and it is possible this arose from lack of knowledge rather than a genuine custom. Therefore it is proper to rule that liver too must be fully roasted before cooking. Nevertheless, for one who drinks the medicinal beverage (ashva) and eats roasted meat in a cooked dish over a long period, one may be lenient to roast only halfway and then cook, since if fully roasted its fat would drain away entirely, leaving no meat flavor in the dish, and since they drink the beverage for health reasons, leniency is granted them.
takeaways: Meat roasted without salting requires full roasting (not half) before cooking, unlike the loose custom that exists regarding liver.
For patients drinking a certain medicinal beverage who insist on roasted meat in a cooked dish — leniency to half-roast was granted, for health reasons.

paragraphs: Basar shello nimlach, o shennimlach beodo beshappud venitzla miyyad - tob lehizzaher shello yasiru hashshappud shettachub bo habbasar min haesh kede letaqqen haesh o lesibba acheret qodem shennitzla habbasar chatzi tzeliyyato. v"g depoh irenu nahagu hetter bazeh, veyesh lahem al mah sheyyismoku, im kol zeh baal-nepesh yachmir lehizzaher bazeh, vetabo alayv beraka.

clarification.explanation: Meat not salted at all, or salted lightly while already skewered and roasted immediately — one should be careful not to remove it from the fire (to adjust the fire or for any other reason) before it has been roasted at least halfway. In some places the custom was to be lenient about this, and they have grounds to rely upon, but a person who is stringent with himself (a "ba'al nefesh") and careful about this is praiseworthy.
takeaways: It is good to be careful not to remove unsalted meat from the fire before it has reached at least a half-roasting, even though some are lenient about this.

paragraphs: Basar zeh shetztzolin belo melicha, o shennimlach meat beodo bishpud, en notenin kikkar lechem vekayyotze tachat hatztzali kede leqabbel shumman hannotep mimmennu. gam lekattechilla asur litzlot basar shennimlach kedino qodem tzeliyya im basar shennitzla belo melicha; ubediabad muttar. veyesh oserin lekattechilla litten betzalim bishpud ben chatikat basar lachatikat basar velitzlotam yachad, veyesh mattirin; vehammachmir, tabo alayv beraka. veayyen machaziq beraka, siman "g, ot t"v.

clarification.explanation: Meat roasted without salting (or with a little salt scattered just before immediate roasting) — it is forbidden to place a loaf of bread or similar item beneath it on the fire to absorb the dripping fat, since the bread would absorb the blood drawn out from the meat. Likewise, as the primary practice, it is forbidden to roast together meat properly salted (which still retains blood the salt did not fully remove) with meat roasted without any salting at all — but after the fact, if they were roasted together, it is permitted. Regarding placing onions on the skewer between pieces of meat and roasting them together — some forbid this as the primary practice and some permit it, and one who is stringent is blessed.
takeaways: It is forbidden to place bread beneath unsalted roasting meat to absorb the dripping fat.
It is forbidden as the primary practice to roast properly salted meat together with unsalted meat (permitted after the fact); onions between meat pieces are disputed.

paragraphs: Basar shennimlach kedarko liqdera sheshshaha shiur melicha verotzeh litzloto, tzarik sheyyedichennu qodem tzeliyya hadacha gemura shelosh peamim kaasher yedichennu liqdera. veim shakach velo hiddicho qodem tzeliyya, yedichennu achar tzeliyya, vegam atta yedichennu shelosh peamim kedin hadacha dilachar melicha; mihu, basar shehudach hadacha harishona min haddam shealayv keshehebio min haqqatztzab, veaach"k techabo beshappud umalechu beodo tachub beshappud, vetzala oto tekep umiyyad - en tzarik lahadicho achar tzeliyya, deen lachush laddam sheal hammelach; mippene shehu achar sheppizzer alayv hammelach bihyoto beshappud, hinnicho tekep umiyyad al haesh, veaz haesh monea hammelach millibloa haddam. umah shennireh laenayim mohal adom al habbasar achar tzeliyya, eno ella chamar basar. veayyen peri chadash veshulchan gabohha; veken hamminhag poh irenu leekol hatztzali hazzeh belo hadacha. bammeh debarim amurim? kesherotzeh leakelo tzali, abal im rotzeh lebashshelo achar tzeliyya, tzarik lahadicho qodem sheyyebashshelennu; vehattaam meboar b"bet-yosep", siman "g, dehu mishshum marit haayin. veayyen peri chadash besiman "g ubesiman "v, seip qatan t"z. veken nohagim poh bagdad lehaddicha hakkabed achar tzeliyyato kesherotzim lebashshelo.

clarification.explanation: Meat salted in the normal manner before cooking (in a pot) and left in salt for the required time to draw out the blood, which one now wishes to roast — must be rinsed thoroughly three times before roasting, just as before cooking. And if one forgot to rinse before roasting, one should rinse after roasting, likewise three times. But meat rinsed once of blood when brought from the butcher, and then skewered and lightly salted while on the skewer, and roasted immediately — need not be rinsed after roasting, since the salt did not have time to absorb blood before the fire stopped it; the reddish appearance seen on the meat after roasting is merely "meat juice" and not blood. This is the Baghdad custom — to eat such a roast without rinsing. But if one wishes to cook this meat after roasting, it must indeed be rinsed first — for reasons of appearance — and this is also the Baghdad custom regarding liver: it is rinsed after roasting when one wishes to cook it.
takeaways: Meat properly salted for cooking that one wishes to roast requires a triple rinse before (or after) roasting.
Meat rinsed only once and roasted immediately with a little salt on the skewer need not be rinsed after roasting to eat as a roast, but must be rinsed if one wishes to cook it afterward.

paragraphs: Basar sheshshaha shelosha yamim meet leet belo melicha, nityabbesh damo betoko, velo yatza od "y melicha apillu im yittenuhu bemayim posherin; veim bishshelu – neesar; vaapillu shello bishshelo legamre, ella sam oto biqdera shehayyad soledet bah, asur kedin basar shello nimlach, abal muttar litzloto uleakelo, veyesh lemalecho qetzat qodem tzeliyya.

clarification.explanation: Meat left three full days (day for day) without salting — the blood inside it dries and can no longer be drawn out by salting, even if soaked in lukewarm water. If it is cooked this way, it is forbidden. And even if not fully cooked but only placed in a pot at a heat that would burn a hand, this is already forbidden like unsalted meat. However, it is permitted to roast such meat and eat it, and it is preferable to salt it lightly before roasting.
takeaways: Meat left three days without salting is forbidden for cooking (even partial heating in a pot), but permitted for roasting and eating, preferably with a little salt first.

paragraphs: Basar zeh, achar shetztzelao name lo yebashshelennu, v"p shemmelacho qodem tzeliyya melicha gemura shehu shiur deeno neekol mechamat milcho. vekol zeh lekattechilla, abal bediabad im bishshelo achar tzeliyya, muttar. veim hu ereb-shabbat veyesh sheat haddechaq, sheen motze basar acher liqnot, az gam lekattechilla muttar lebashshelo achar tzeliyya. vehu haddin letzorek seudat mitzva name shari lebashshelo lekattechilla achar tzeliyya. veayyen keneset haggedola umishbetzot zahab veshiyyure beraka. veken hu haddin behepsed merubbeh, yesh lehattir bishshul achar tzeliyya. ayyen "zera-emet", yoreh dea, siman k"b.

clarification.explanation: Meat left three days and then roasted (as mentioned in the previous halacha) — it is forbidden to also cook it after roasting, even if it was fully and adequately salted before roasting. This is the law as the primary practice, but after the fact, if it was cooked after roasting, it is permitted. And if it is Sabbath eve and there is great difficulty (no other meat available to buy), then even as the primary practice it is permitted to cook it after roasting. The same law applies for the sake of a mitzvah meal — it is permitted as the primary practice to cook it after roasting. Likewise in a case of great monetary loss, one may be lenient to cook it after roasting.
takeaways: Meat left three days and roasted — forbidden as the primary practice to cook afterward, but permitted after the fact, or in pressing situations (Sabbath eve, a mitzvah meal, great loss).

paragraphs: Basar zeh sheshshaha g' yamim belo melicha - im nimlach bikli sheeno menuqqab, dino kedin basar dealema, deim shaha bakkeli shiur sheyyittenu mayim al haesh veyukal leharticha, az neesar habbasar hazzeh gam letzali.

clarification.explanation: Meat left three days without salting — if it was salted in a non-perforated vessel (so the liquids do not drain out), its law is like ordinary meat: if it remained in this vessel long enough to have boiled water on a fire, the meat is forbidden even for roasting.
takeaways: Old meat salted in a sealed (non-draining) vessel and left there a long time is forbidden even for roasting, not just cooking.

paragraphs: Basar zeh sheshshaha shelosha yamim belo melicha - im milcho im basar harauy limlicha shemmolecho lehotzi damo, hinneh adayin yesh hetter lebasar zeh sheshshaha - taqqana bitzliyya. vehabbasar hashsheni harauy limlicha shemmalechu lehotzi damo, muttar achar melicha, ben bebishshul, ben bitzliyya.

clarification.explanation: Meat left three days without salting — if it was salted together with other fresh meat fit for ordinary salting (to draw out its blood), there is still a remedy for this old meat: it can be rectified through roasting. And the other, fresh meat, properly salted to draw out its blood, is permitted after salting both for cooking and for roasting.
takeaways: Old meat salted together with fresh meat — the old meat can only be rectified by roasting; the fresh meat is permitted for both cooking and roasting.

paragraphs: Shumman shel basar veshumman shel avvaz, dino kemo habbasar, demachziqin bo dam; veim shaha shelosha yamim belo melicha, neesar bebishshul kedin habbasar, ak kevan dehu shumman lo epshar litzloto, ki nimmocha; veim yearebu beshumman acher lebattelo, gam zeh i epshar, deqayma lan: en mebattelin issur lekattechilla. ketzad yaaseh? yimlachennu techilla melicha gemura, veaach"k yebashshelennu bemayim sheyyesh bahem shishshim peamim keneged zeh hashshumman; veaz yiqqach hashshumman shehu tzap lemala vehu muttar, shekkebar nitbattel issur dam beshishshim; veen bazeh mishshum en mebattelin issur lekattechilla, dedame lehagala, shehu asa kede lehaplit haissur; velaken tzarik sheyyishpok otam hammayim leibbud velo yehaneh mehem; ken katab haggaon chavvat daat za"l, vehiskim immo haggaon "yad-eprayim" za"l.

clarification.explanation: The fat of meat or of a goose has the same law as the meat itself, since it too holds blood inside it. If left three days without salting, it is forbidden for cooking exactly like meat, but unlike meat — it cannot be rectified through roasting, since fat melts and dissolves in fire. Mixing it with other fat to nullify it is also not possible, since there is a rule forbidding the deliberate nullification of a prohibition from the outset. The solution: salt the fat with a full salting, then cook it in water containing sixty times the fat's volume; afterward, take the fat that floats to the top — it is permitted, since the blood in it has already been nullified in sixty. This is not considered "deliberately nullifying a prohibition," since the action resembles purging (whose purpose is to expel the forbidden substance, not deliberately nullify it) — and therefore the water used for this must be poured out and not benefited from.
takeaways: Fat left three days without salting is forbidden for cooking, and cannot be rectified by roasting (since it melts) or by mixing with other fat.
The solution: salt it, then cook it in water with sixty times its volume; the floating fat is permitted, but the water must be poured out, not used.

paragraphs: Lekattechilla en lehashhot habbasar shelosha yamim belo melicha, dechayeshinan shemma yebashshelennu. veim hishha oto beshogeg, tzarik litzloto tekep, dechayeshinan dilma mishtele umebashshel leh, vekannizkar "bashshemesh-tzedaqa", siman t"l. ak hakkabed vehakkechal, muttar lehashhotan, mishshum diblav haki asurim bebishshul, ubevadday yitzlennu. v"g dekabed muttar lebashshelo achar tzeliyya, mikkol maqom kevan degam habbasar muttar bediabad lebashshelo achar tzeliyya, la chayeshinan leha dekatab "pitche-teshuba" beshem "chamude-daniyyel", siman l"d.

clarification.explanation: As the primary practice, meat should not be left three days without salting, out of concern that people might forget and cook it. And if it was left this way inadvertently, it should be roasted immediately, out of concern that people might forget and also cook it. However, liver and spleen may be left longer, since they are in any case forbidden to cook (even fresh) before roasting, and therefore there is no concern that people would cook them by mistake — they will certainly roast them. And although liver may also be cooked after roasting, this raises no additional concern, since ordinary meat too is permitted after the fact to cook after roasting, and therefore there is no need to be concerned for the stricter view on this point.
takeaways: Meat should not be left three days without salting, out of concern for forgetfulness; if it happened, roast it immediately.
Liver and spleen, always forbidden to cook before roasting anyway, may be left longer, since there is no concern about forgetting to roast them.

paragraphs: Basar sheshshaha belo melicha, vechal yom shelishi shello beshabbat - yesh mattirin lishrot habbasar hazzeh bemayim beshabbat, kede shello yeaser bebishshul achar shabbat; veyesh oserin lishroto beshabbat apillu "y nakeri; veyesh oserin "y yisrael umattirin "y nakeri, verauy lehorot kedibrehem lehattir "y nakeri, ak tob sheyyaaseh shebut dishbut, dehaynu: hayisrael yomar lenakeri shehu yomar lenakeri acher lishroto bemayim. vehachenvani hammoker basar shennishar lo basar harbeh, sheim lo yasharnu bemayim beshabbat yaabru alayv shelosha yamim, veit leh peseda tuba, shetztzarik lemakero bezol meod, deen neekol ella tzali, hare zeh muttar lishroto "y nakeri lekulle alema. veayyen "shebut-yaaqob", cheleq g, siman k"b.

clarification.explanation: Meat left without salting, whose third day falls on the Sabbath — some permit soaking the meat in water on the Sabbath itself so it does not become forbidden for cooking after the Sabbath's conclusion, and some forbid soaking it on the Sabbath even through a gentile, with an intermediate view: forbidden through a Jew but permitted through a gentile. The ruling is to follow the view permitting it through a gentile, though it is good to do a "double indirection" — that is, the Jew tells one gentile to tell a second gentile to soak the meat in water (a doubled instruction). Regarding a shopkeeper left with much meat, who if he does not soak it in water on the Sabbath will have three days pass and suffer a great monetary loss (since such meat can only be eaten roasted and sells for very little) — he is permitted to soak the meat through a gentile according to all opinions.
takeaways: Meat whose third day falls on the Sabbath — the authorities disagree on soaking it in water; the ruling: permitted through a gentile, preferably with double indirection.
A shopkeeper facing significant financial loss may soak the meat through a gentile according to all opinions.

paragraphs: Basar shennimlach, asur lekattechilla lehashhoto bemilcho y"b shaot, shehu shiur pelitat kol tziro, ella yedichennu qodem y"b shaot; ubediabad muttar apillu im shaha bemilcho meet leet o yoter. veim habbasar nimlach beereb-shabbat veshakechu lahadicho venizkeru beyom-shabbat, asur lahadicho "y nakeri, ella yishshaer ad motzae-shabbat veyaddichuhu, dezeh chashib kediabad, ukemo shettab b"lechem-happanim".

clarification.explanation: Salted meat should not, as the primary practice, be left in its salt for twelve hours (the time needed for it to release all its blood), but must be rinsed before twelve hours pass. But after the fact, even if it remained in its salt a full day or more, it is permitted. If the meat was salted on the Sabbath eve and they forgot to rinse it, and only remembered on the Sabbath — it is forbidden to rinse it through a gentile; rather it should be left as is until the Sabbath's conclusion and rinsed then, since this situation is considered "after the fact."
takeaways: Meat should not, as the primary practice, be left in its salt more than twelve hours, but after the fact, even a longer time is permitted.
If forgotten to rinse before the Sabbath, it should not be rinsed through a gentile on the Sabbath, but left until the Sabbath's conclusion.

paragraphs: Basar shennimlach venityabbesh qodem shehedichuhu hadacha acharona, "g sheyyesh shishshim neged hammelach shealayv bevadday, kevan dikbar nityabbesh, mikkol maqom tzarik lehizzaher lahadicho qodem bishshul. vetob shettihyeh hadachat basar hayyabesh beposherin, ki happosherin tobim min hatztzonenim lehasir haddam vehammelach shennityabbesh al habbasar. veyizzaher meod sheyyihyu posherin velo chammin shehayyad soledet bahem, deim ken mah moil bahadacha zo, dahare zeh have kemo bishshul?

clarification.explanation: Meat that was salted and dried out before the final rinsing could be performed — even though it certainly contains sixty times the amount of salt on it, one must nevertheless be careful to rinse it before cooking, since it has already dried. It is good for the rinsing of such dry meat to be done with lukewarm water rather than cold, since lukewarm water is better for removing dried blood and salt. But one must be very careful that the water be only lukewarm and not hot enough to burn a hand — since if so, this very rinsing act would be considered cooking (and would not help).
takeaways: Salted meat that dried before the final rinse must still be rinsed before cooking, preferably with lukewarm (not cold or truly hot) water.

paragraphs: Yesh bene-adam darkan limshok shekar temarim min shekar sheqqorin bearbe "rg'yy" (seppiret, zeat temarim), shemmoshekim mimmennu "y qanim shekar chashub sheqqorin "dubbeara" (mubchar); vedarkam lehannicha tarnegolet shechuta betok haddud shebbo hashshekar sheqqorin "rg'yy", kede sheyyetze hashshekar sheqqorin "dubrh" chashub meod; ak en rotzim limloach otah beameram, im yimlechu otah, yitqalqel hashshekar. ubazeh hashshekar sheqqorin "reg'yy" yesh shishshim al hattarnegolet - heeleti bitshuba bsh"q "rab-pealim" deasur lemebad ken lekattechilla "g deyesh shishshim, veheerakti bedabar zeh sham bs"d, vekatabti deim i epshar lo limloach, yitzleh hattarnegolet chatzi tzeliyya, veyannichenna betok hashshekar.

clarification.explanation: Some people produce a type of date beer from a base beer called in Arabic "raji'i" (date sweat), from which a higher-quality beer called "dubara" is extracted through reeds. They are accustomed to place a slaughtered chicken (without salting) into the vessel with the beer, so the quality beer ("dubara") comes out better, but they do not want to salt the chicken, claiming it would spoil the beer. The Ben Ish Chai, in his book "Rav Pe'alim," ruled that this is forbidden as the primary practice, even though there is sixty times the chicken's volume in the beer (which would nullify the blood). He proposed a solution: if it is truly impossible to salt the chicken, one should roast it halfway (which draws out some of the blood through the fire) and then place it in the beer.
takeaways: It is forbidden as the primary practice to place unsalted fowl into beer to improve its flavor, even with sixty times its volume present.
The proposed solution: half-roast the fowl before placing it in the beer, to draw out some of the blood first.

paragraphs: Dam hannimtza bechalab shechalabo min hatztzon o min haez - im hu mareh adom, yesh bazeh issur dam kemo shekkatebu haacharonim beshem "nachalat-shiba", veken katab harab "chinnuk-bet-yeuddeh", siman l"ch. mihu, yimmatze poh irenu bachaliba harishona o sheniyya shettihyeh merechelim o izzim achar ledatam, sheyyehe mareh hechalab eno laban gamur, ella noteh leyaroq, shehu givvun sheqqorin bearbi "atztzippor" (tzahob) - en chashash bazeh, dela aseru ella mareh adom, abal mareh yaroq en bo chashash kelal. vbsh"q "rab-pealim" hebeti reaya lazeh missiman qp"ch, seip ', sheppasaq mera"n za"l: mareh yaroq apillu kemareh hashshaava o hazzahab, vekol-shekken hayyaroq kekarti o kaasabim, tahor, ayyen sham. veayyen sha"k za"l sham, seip qatan d, yeuyyan sham. nimtza, apillu bedam nidda hutteru marot ellu shel yaroq, shehem mareh hashshaava o hazzahab o etrog o chelmon betza vekayyotze, vekannizkar bashsha"k za"l. al-ken hechalab hazzeh en bo chashash, umuttar hu vezeh barur.

clarification.explanation: If blood is found in the milk of sheep or goats, this carries the prohibition of blood if the blood's color is red, as the later authorities wrote. But there is a case where, in the first or second milking after the animal gives birth, the milk's color is not fully white but leans toward greenish-yellow — and here there is no concern at all, since the prohibition of blood applies only to a red appearance, not a green one. The Ben Ish Chai brings proof from the laws of niddah: Maran ruled that a greenish appearance, even like wax or gold, and all the more so green like leeks or grass, is pure and not considered niddah blood. If so, in this milk too, whose color leans toward greenish-yellow (like wax, gold, an etrog, or egg yolk) — there is no concern of prohibition at all, and it is entirely and clearly permitted.
takeaways: Blood in milk that is red in color is forbidden; but milk whose color leans toward greenish-yellow (as in the first milking after birth) carries no concern at all, as also learned from the laws of niddah blood-color.
